17600:
To yank something means to pull it suddenly and with force. It is not a slow, gentle, or gradual pull. A yank is sharp, quick, and energetic — done in one swift motion.

Think of it this way: if you pull a drawer open normally, that is just a pull. But if you grab it and rip it open in one sharp, sudden move — that is a yank.
The Two Things That Make a Pull a "Yank"

Both of these qualities must be present:

1. Suddenness — It happens fast, in a flash. There is no build-up, no slow increase in force. It goes from zero to full force almost instantly.

2. Force — It is not gentle. A yank carries energy and strength behind it.

Remove either one, and it stops being a yank. A slow, forceful pull is not a yank. A quick but feather-light tug is not a yank either. A yank is both at once.

• The dentist yanked the tooth out in one quick motion.
  • She yanked the blanket off him and told him to wake up.
  • The dog got excited and yanked the leash right out of her hand.
  • He yanked the door open and stormed out of the room.
  • The child yanked his mother's sleeve to get her attention.

In every case above, notice the same feeling: a sudden, forceful, clean pull — one motion, no hesitation.

Since you are a learner, it helps to know where "yank" sits among words that feel similar:

Pull is the broad, general word. It can be slow or fast, gentle or hard. Yank is a specific type of pull — the sudden and forceful kind.

Tug is a pull too, but a tug is often smaller and may be repeated multiple times (like tugging at someone's sleeve again and again). A yank is typically one sharp, decisive move.

Jerk is very close to yank. Both are sudden and forceful. However, "jerk" often feels rougher, more uncontrolled, or even violent. A "yank" feels more purposeful — like someone doing it intentionally to get a result.

Snatch focuses more on grabbing something quickly, while yank focuses on the pulling motion itself.

Yank is very commonly used with small direction or position words to tell you where or how something is being pulled. These combinations are natural and widely used:

  • Yank out — to pull something out of a place (yank out a weed from the ground, yank out a plug from a socket)
  • Yank off — to pull something off a surface (yank off a bandage)
  • Yank open — to pull something open forcefully (yank open a stuck drawer)
  • Yank away — to pull something away from someone or something (she yanked the phone away from him)
  • Yank free — to pull until you are free from something (he yanked himself free from the rope)
Figurative Uses (When "Yank" Does Not Mean a Physical Pull)

Language is creative, and "yank" has grown beyond just physical pulling. Here are the important non-literal uses:

1. To remove something suddenly and without much warning

When something is "yanked," it means it was taken away or removed abruptly — often by someone in authority, and often before anyone expected it.

  • The television network yanked the show after just two episodes because ratings were poor.
  • The government yanked his licence after the investigation.
  • The product was yanked from shelves as soon as the safety issue was discovered.

The image here is the same: something that was in place gets pulled out suddenly, just like a physical yank.

2. "Yank someone's chain" (informal phrase)

This means to tease someone, fool them, or deliberately mislead them — usually in a playful but sometimes annoying way. It is like pretending to pull someone along in a false direction.

  • "Are you serious, or are you just yanking my chain?"
  • "Stop yanking his chain — he actually believed you!"

3. "Yank someone around" (informal)

This means to treat someone poorly by making them do unnecessary things, giving them conflicting information, or wasting their time — essentially, not being straight or fair with them.

  • "I've been calling customer service for a week and they keep yanking me around."

Yank is an informal, everyday word. You will hear it in normal conversation, in books, in movies, and in casual writing. It is not a formal or technical word. You would not normally use it in a business report or an academic paper — in those settings, you would say "remove," "withdraw," or "pull" instead. But in everyday speech and writing, yank is perfectly natural and widely understood.
The Overall Feel of the Word

If you had to capture "yank" in a feeling, it is the feeling of something being ripped away cleanly and quickly — whether that is a weed from the ground, a tooth from a mouth, a show from a schedule, or the truth from someone who has been fooling you. It always carries that same energy: sudden, direct, and forceful.
17601: The word "yap" as a noun carries several related meanings, all tied together by one central idea: something sharp, high-pitched, and not particularly meaningful. Here is every sense of the word explained fully.
Meaning 1 — A Short, Sharp, High-Pitched Bark

This is the original and most literal meaning. A yap is the quick, thin, piercing bark that a small dog makes.

Imagine the difference between a large dog's deep, powerful "WOOF" and the rapid, high-pitched "yip! yip! yip!" of a tiny Chihuahua or Yorkshire Terrier. That shrill little bark is a yap.

A yap is always:

  • High-pitched — not deep or rumbling
  • Short and sharp — not a long, drawn-out howl
  • Often repeated rapidly in quick succession
  • Strongly associated with small dogs

"The little dog let out a yap every time someone knocked on the door."
"I heard a sudden yap from the corner — the puppy had gotten startled."
Meaning 2 — Foolish, Pointless, or Irritating Talk (Informal)

In informal English, "yap" refers to excessive, meaningless chatter — talking a lot without saying anything useful or important.

The tone here is dismissive or slightly annoyed. Calling someone's speech "yap" suggests it is noise, not substance — like that small dog barking at nothing.

"I've had enough of his yap — he never actually says anything."
"All that yap about being the best player, and then he lost in the first round."

This is a very natural and common usage in everyday informal speech.
Meaning 3 — The Mouth (Informal, Can Sound Rude)

"Yap" can also directly mean a person's mouth, especially in the context of talking too much or being told to stop.

"Shut your yap!" is a blunt, informal way of saying "Shut your mouth!" or "Stop talking!"

"He opened his yap at exactly the wrong moment."
"Keep your yap shut and listen for once."

This is casual and can sound aggressive or rude depending on tone. It is not suitable for polite or formal situations. The logic is simple: the mouth is the thing the yap (chatter) comes out of, so the two meanings blur together.
Meaning 4 — A Foolish or Worthless Person (Informal, Less Common)

Less commonly, and more in older or regional British and Australian usage, "yap" can describe a foolish, dim-witted, or contemptible person — someone who talks without sense.

"Don't take advice from that yap — he doesn't know what he's talking about."

You will not encounter this meaning as often today, but it is worth knowing so you are never caught off guard.

All four meanings grow from the same root idea: something noisy, sharp, and lacking in real substance.

  • A dog's yap = a sharp, trivial noise
  • Human yap (talk) = sharp, trivial words
  • The yap (mouth) = the organ that produces the trivial noise
  • A yap (person) = someone whose ideas and words are trivial

Once you see this thread running through all the meanings, the word becomes very easy to remember.

Plural: Simply "yaps" — "The yaps of the dogs echoed through the street."

Formality: Meanings 2, 3, and 4 are all informal. Avoid them in formal writing or professional settings.

Modern slang: Among younger speakers today, especially online, "yap" has become extremely popular to describe someone who talks endlessly. Phrases like "he's on a yap" (he's in the middle of a long, rambling speech) or calling someone "a yapper" (a person who yaps constantly) are very common and carry a humorous tone rather than an aggressive one.

Related forms: It helps to know that "yapping" (the action) and "yapper" (a person or dog that yaps) are the most common related words you will encounter in the wild.
17602: The word yard has several distinct meanings. Each one is used in a different context, but they are all common enough that you will encounter them in everyday reading or conversation. Here is every meaning explained clearly.

A yard is a fixed unit used to measure length or distance. It equals 3 feet, or 36 inches. To give you a rough sense of size, one yard is just a little bit shorter than one metre.

You will see this meaning used in everyday life when measuring things like:

  • Fabric or cloth ("I need two yards of silk")
  • Distances on a road or field ("The car stopped just 10 yards away")
  • Grass, fencing, or construction materials

In American football, the field is 100 yards long, which is one of the most famous uses of this unit. This meaning of "yard" is especially common in the United States, the United Kingdom, and a few other countries that use the imperial system of measurement.
2. An Enclosed Area of Land Near a Building

A yard can also mean an outdoor area of ground that belongs to, or is attached to, a building. Think of it as the open land that surrounds or sits beside a structure.

This meaning is very flexible. A yard can be:

  • Paved (covered with stone, concrete, or bricks), or
  • Grassy and open (like a garden or lawn)

You will often hear this combined with another word to describe where the yard is:

  • Front yard — the open area of land at the front of a house, facing the street
  • Back yard (backyard) — the outdoor area behind a house; in many countries this is where families relax, barbecue, or let their children play
  • Side yard — a narrow strip of land running along the side of a house

In American English especially, when someone says "yard," they often mean the grassy area around their home. Children "play in the yard." Dogs "run around the yard." Families "sit out in the yard" on summer evenings.

In British English, a yard tends to suggest a paved outdoor space (a courtyard), while a grassy area around a home is more likely to be called a garden.
3. An Enclosed Space Used for a Specific Activity or Work

A yard can refer to a specially designated enclosed area where a particular kind of work is done, or where things are stored. This is where the word gets combined with other words to name many specific places you already know:

  • Shipyard — a large area by the water where ships are built or repaired
  • Junkyard (also called a scrap yard or salvage yard) — a place where old, broken, or unwanted vehicles and metal objects are collected, stored, and often recycled
  • Lumberyard (or timber yard) — a place where cut wood and timber are stored and sold
  • Stockyard — a large enclosed space where cattle, pigs, sheep, or other farm animals are temporarily kept, often before being sold or transported
  • Railyard (or railway yard / train yard) — a large area of land with many railway tracks where trains are stored, sorted, assembled, and directed to their correct routes
  • Brickyard — a place where bricks are made or stored
  • Coalyard — a place where coal is stored and sold
  • Schoolyard — the open outdoor area within or beside a school where children play during breaks
  • Churchyard — the enclosed ground surrounding a church, which often contains graves and burial stones

In all these cases, the word "yard" carries the idea of an enclosed, purposeful space — not just random open land, but a place set aside for a job or a use.

In the context of prisons, the yard (almost always said with "the") refers to the outdoor area inside a prison where inmates are allowed to go outside, get fresh air, and exercise. You will commonly come across this meaning in books, films, and TV shows about prison life. For example: "The prisoners walked out into the yard."
5. A Horizontal Pole on a Ship's Mast (Nautical)

In sailing and maritime contexts, a yard is a long horizontal pole or spar that is attached crossways to the mast (the tall vertical pole) of a sailing ship. Sails are spread out and hung from this pole. When you see old paintings or illustrations of tall sailing ships with large square sails stretched wide, those sails hang from yards. This is a more specialized meaning, mostly used in nautical, historical, or literary contexts. You may also see the related word yardarm, which refers to either of the two outer ends of this pole.

You may hear the phrase Scotland Yard — this is the popular name for the headquarters of London's Metropolitan Police. When people say "Scotland Yard is investigating the case," they simply mean the London police. This is a proper name, not a general use of the word, but it is worth knowing because you will encounter it frequently in British news, crime novels, and films.

In informal American English slang, a yard can mean one hundred dollars. This usage is mostly heard in casual speech or street slang — for example, "That cost me two yards" means "That cost me two hundred dollars." You are unlikely to see this in formal writing, but you may encounter it in fiction, films, or informal conversation.

ContextWhat "yard" means

To summarise simply: yard is a word with a range of meanings tied together by two broad ideas — measurement and enclosed space. When measuring, a yard is 36 inches. When talking about space, a yard is an outdoor area attached to a building or set aside for a specific purpose. The specific meaning always becomes clear from the context around the word. Once you know all these meanings, you will find the word "yard" easy to understand wherever you meet it.
17603:
Before understanding "yardage," you need to know that a yard is a unit of measurement equal to 3 feet (or 36 inches). It's used widely in the United States and some other countries to measure distance or length.

Now, yardage simply means an amount, length, or distance measured in yards. The suffix "-age" signals that we're talking about a quantity or total of something — just like "mileage" means an amount of miles, and "footage" means an amount of feet.

So yardage answers the question: "How many yards?"
The Different Contexts Where "Yardage" Is Used

The word "yardage" appears in several distinct areas of life. Each one uses the word in a slightly different but related way.

1. Fabric and Sewing

This is one of the most common everyday uses of "yardage." When you go to a fabric store, cloth is sold by the yard. The total amount of fabric you buy or need for a project is called its yardage.

Think of it this way: if a dress requires 4 yards of cloth, a seamstress would say, "I need 4 yards of yardage" or simply "What's the yardage needed for this pattern?"

Yardage in this context tells you how much fabric is involved — whether you're buying it, measuring it, or estimating it for a project.

  • "Make sure you buy enough yardage before you start cutting."
  • "The yardage for this quilt is about 6 yards."

2. American Football

In American football, yardage is one of the most frequently used words in the sport. The entire game is built around gaining yards — teams try to move the ball forward, 10 yards at a time, to eventually score.

Here, yardage refers to the number of yards a team or player gains (or loses) during a game or a specific period of play.

There are several types of yardage talked about in football:

  • Rushing yardage — yards gained by running with the ball.
  • Passing yardage — yards gained by throwing the ball.
  • Total yardage — the combined yards gained overall.
  • Penalty yardage — yards lost because of rule violations.

Examples:

  • "The running back had 120 yards of rushing yardage in that game."
  • "Their total offensive yardage was over 400 yards."

Yardage here is essentially a performance statistic — it tells you how much ground was covered.

3. Golf

In golf, yardage tells you how far away the hole (or any target on the course) is, measured in yards.

Every golf hole has a yardage — it's the distance from where you tee off (start) to the hole itself. Golfers use yardage constantly to decide which club to use and how hard to swing.

  • "This hole has a yardage of 420 yards — it's a tough one."
  • "Check your yardage book to see how far the bunker is."

Golf courses also publish a total yardage — the combined distance of all 18 holes added together. A course might be described as playing at "6,800 yards."

Yardage in golf is essentially a precise distance measurement that shapes every decision a golfer makes on the course.

4. General Use (Distance or Length in Yards)

Outside of sports and fabric, "yardage" can simply mean any distance or measurement expressed in yards in a general sense.

  • "They measured the yardage of the field before laying the turf."
  • "What's the yardage from the house to the fence?"

This is the broadest and most literal use of the word — it's just asking or stating how many yards something is.

5. Livestock and Stockyards (Less Common)

This is a rarer, older meaning. A stockyard is a large enclosed area where cattle and other livestock are kept temporarily. In this context, yardage refers to the fee or charge paid for keeping animals in such a yard.

  • "The farmer paid a yardage fee to keep his cattle at the stockyard overnight."

Think of it like a parking fee, but for animals. This meaning is mostly used in agricultural and farming contexts and is not common in everyday conversation today.

Here is the big picture: yardage always involves yards as a unit, but what it's measuring depends on the situation:

  • In fabric/sewing, it's the amount of cloth.
  • In football, it's how far the ball has traveled or been moved.
  • In golf, it's how far a target or hole is.
  • In general use, it's simply any length or distance in yards.
  • In livestock contexts, it's a fee for using a yard (enclosure).

The word is always a quantity or measure — never an action, never a person, never a place. It answers the question "how many yards?" or "what is the yard-based measurement here?"

Think of yardage as the "yard version" of the word mileage. Just as mileage tells you how many miles a car has traveled or how far away something is in miles, yardage tells you the same thing — but in yards. Once you see that parallel, the word becomes very intuitive across all its uses.
17604: "Yardarm" is a sailing and nautical word. To understand it, you first need to picture an old-fashioned sailing ship — the kind with tall masts and large fabric sails. This word describes a specific part of that ship.

On a sailing ship, a yard (or "yardarm's parent structure") is a long, horizontal wooden pole that is attached to the mast — the tall vertical pole at the center of the ship. This horizontal pole crosses the mast roughly at a right angle, like a giant "T" or a cross. Sails hang down from it.

Think of it like this: if the mast is the vertical bar of a cross, the yard is the horizontal bar.

A yardarm is either of the two outer ends of a yard — the tips that stick out to the left and right of the mast.

So the yard is the entire long horizontal pole. The yardarm is specifically the outermost portion of that pole, on either side. Each yard has two yardarms: one on the left side (port) and one on the right side (starboard).

Picture it: a mast goes up vertically. A long pole goes through it horizontally. The far-left tip of that pole is a yardarm. The far-right tip is also a yardarm.
How It Was Actually Used on a Ship

In the age of sail (roughly 1400s–1800s), yardarms served several real purposes:

  1. Supporting sails. The sails were attached to the yard and hung below it. The yardarms defined the full width of that sail area.
  2. Flying signals. Flags, signal lights, and pennants were often hoisted up to the yardarm to communicate with other ships — since the ends of the yard were high up and visible from far away.
  3. Rigging work. Sailors would sometimes have to climb out to the yardarm — a dangerous job — to handle ropes and sails in all kinds of weather.
The Dark Historical Use: Hanging from the Yardarm

One of the most historically significant uses of the yardarm was as a place of execution at sea.

When a sailor committed a serious crime — such as mutiny (rebelling against the captain), desertion, or piracy — the punishment could be death by hanging. Because there were no gallows on a ship, a rope would be tied to the yardarm, and the condemned person would be hanged from that high outer tip of the horizontal pole.

This was done because the yardarm was:

  • High enough off the deck to serve as a gallows
  • Visible to the entire crew, making the punishment a warning to others
  • Already a sturdy, load-bearing structure

This is why you'll often encounter the phrase "hanged from the yardarm" or "hang from the yardarm" in historical novels, sea stories, and expressions referring to punishment or doom.

Example: "The captain warned that any man who betrayed the ship would be hanged from the yardarm before sunrise."
The Famous Idiom: "The Sun Is Over the Yardarm"

This is the most commonly used expression involving "yardarm" in modern English, and it's worth knowing well.

Meaning: It is late enough in the day that it is socially acceptable to have an alcoholic drink.

Origin: On ships sailing in northern latitudes, the sun — when low on the horizon in the morning — was below the level of the yardarm when viewed from the deck. As the day progressed and the sun climbed higher in the sky, it would eventually rise above the yardarm. This moment (roughly mid-to-late morning, around 11 AM) was informally used by sailors as a signal that the working part of the morning was over and a drink was permissible.

Over time, this phrase moved from ships into everyday speech, where it is used humorously or casually to justify having a drink — especially during the day.

Example: "It's barely noon, but I suppose the sun is over the yardarm somewhere in the world." (Said when someone wants a drink earlier than is typically considered polite.)

Example: "Pour me a whiskey — the sun's well over the yardarm by now."

The phrase can also be used more broadly (and less literally) to mean simply: the right time has come for something.

Here are examples showing the word in different contexts:

  • Literal/nautical: "The sailor edged carefully along the yard and out to the yardarm to untangle the rigging during the storm."
  • Historical/punishment: "Pirates captured by the navy faced a swift trial and were hanged from the yardarm as a warning to others."
  • Idiomatic: "It's five o'clock — the sun is over the yardarm. Time for a drink."
  • Figurative/literary: "He felt as though he were dangling from the yardarm, waiting for the captain's verdict."

A yardarm is the outer end of a horizontal sailing pole (the yard) on a traditional sailing ship — historically used to hang condemned sailors, fly signal flags, and, by way of a famous idiom, to mark the time of day when it becomes acceptable to have a drink.
17605: A yardstick is something used to measure or judge how good, how successful, or how correct something is. Think of it as your personal ruler for making comparisons.

This word carries two meanings: one literal and one figurative. Both are important to know.

Meaning 1 — The Physical Object (Literal)

A yardstick, in its most direct sense, is a flat, straight measuring stick that is exactly one yard long (which equals 36 inches, or about 91 centimetres). It looks like a long, thin ruler. Carpenters, tailors, and craftspeople use it to measure wood, fabric, or any surface with precision.

"She used a yardstick to measure the length of the curtain fabric."

This is the original, straightforward meaning.

Meaning 2 — A Standard for Judgement (Figurative) ⬅ The More Important One

This is where the word truly comes alive, and it is by far the more common way this word is used — in everyday conversation, in newspapers, in business, and in literature.

When used figuratively, a yardstick means a fixed standard, benchmark, or criterion that you use to evaluate, compare, or judge something or someone.

Just like a physical yardstick gives you an exact, unchanging length to measure things against, a figurative yardstick gives you a reliable point of reference to judge whether something is good or bad, successful or unsuccessful, fair or unfair.

Think of it this way:

Imagine you are hiring a chef. You decide that the yardstick for choosing the best chef is how perfectly they can cook a three-course meal in under an hour. Every applicant is judged against that one fixed standard — your yardstick. Anyone who meets it passes. Anyone who doesn't, fails.

The yardstick here is not a physical stick. It is an idea, a rule, or a measure of quality that you use to judge everything else.

• "Profit is not the only yardstick of a company's success."

Here, "yardstick" means the standard being used to decide if a company is doing well. The speaker is saying profit shouldn't be the only measure — other things, like employee happiness or environmental impact, should also matter.

  • "His first novel became the yardstick against which all his later work was measured."

His debut novel set such a high standard that every book he wrote after it was compared to that one to see if it was better, worse, or equal.

  • "Test scores are an imperfect yardstick for measuring a student's intelligence."

Exam results are being used as a measuring standard for intelligence, but the speaker feels this standard is flawed.

For something to be called a yardstick (in the figurative sense), it must do three things:

  1. It must be a standard — a clear, specific point of reference, not something vague.
  2. It must be used for comparison — you measure something else against it.
  3. It must help you make a judgement — it tells you whether something is adequate, superior, or falling short.

These words are close in meaning and can often be used in place of "yardstick":

  • Benchmark — a reference point used to measure performance. Very common in business and technology. (e.g., "The new phone set a benchmark for battery life.")
  • Standard — a level of quality or requirement that is accepted as normal or desirable.
  • Criterion (plural: criteria) — a specific rule or principle by which something is judged. (e.g., "Price is one criterion; quality is another.")
  • Measure — a way of assessing something.
  • Barometer — similar to yardstick but often used when something indicates a broader condition, like a mood or a trend. (e.g., "Box office earnings are a barometer of public taste.")

The subtle difference with yardstick specifically is that it carries a strong sense of a single, definite standard used to judge or compare — like one clear ruler that everyone agrees to measure against.

A yardstick is neutral by nature — it is simply a tool for judgement. But the word is often used in contexts where someone is either:

  • Praising a standard as fair and reliable:

"Customer satisfaction should be the yardstick for every business decision."

  • Criticising a standard as too narrow, unfair, or misleading:

"Using salary alone as the yardstick for a person's worth is deeply misguided."

So pay attention to the surrounding words in a sentence — they'll tell you whether the speaker thinks the yardstick being used is a good or bad one.

A yardstick is a fixed standard used to judge or compare how good, successful, or valid something is — like a ruler, but for ideas, performance, or quality.

Whenever you see or hear this word, ask yourself: "What is being measured, and what is the thing it's being compared against?" Answer those two questions, and the sentence will always make perfect sense.
17606: A yarmulke is a small, round cap — roughly the size of your palm — that Jewish men wear on top of their head. It sits on the crown of the head (the upper-back part), not pulled down over the ears like a regular hat. It covers only a small portion of the head.

It is a soft, brimless cap. It can be made from many materials — velvet, suede, leather, or knitted wool/cotton. It comes in many colors and patterns, though plain black or white ones are common. Some are very small and subtle; others are larger and more visible. The style a person chooses often signals something about their background or level of religious observance.

Jewish men wear it. How often depends on the individual and their Jewish community:

  • Strictly observant (Orthodox) Jewish men wear it every waking hour, all day long, every day of their lives. For them, removing it is unusual.
  • Less strictly observant Jewish men may wear it only during prayer, religious study, or while inside a synagogue (a Jewish house of worship).
  • Some Jewish men choose not to wear it at all — this is considered acceptable in more liberal branches of Judaism.

In some more progressive Jewish communities, women also wear yarmulkes, though this is not traditional.

The yarmulke is worn as an act of respect and humility before God. The idea behind it is that wearing something on your head is a constant, physical reminder that God is above you — above all human beings. It is a way of acknowledging a higher presence at all times.

It is not commanded directly in the written Torah (the Jewish scripture), but it became a deeply rooted tradition over centuries, especially in observant communities, where it eventually took on the weight of religious obligation.

The word yarmulke comes from Yiddish (the language historically spoken by Jews in Eastern Europe). The same item is also called a kippah — this is the Hebrew word for it, and kippah simply means "dome" or "covering." Both words refer to the exact same object. In Israel and in Hebrew-speaking contexts, you'll hear kippah more often. In everyday English conversation, both words are used and understood.
As a symbol of Jewish identity

Beyond its religious meaning, the yarmulke has become one of the most visible and widely recognized symbols of Jewish identity in the world. When someone wears one in public, it is often a conscious, open declaration: I am Jewish, and I am not hiding it.

Because of this, the choice of whether to wear a yarmulke in public can carry personal weight — some Jews see it as an act of pride and courage, especially in parts of the world where being visibly Jewish has historically brought risk.

When a non-Jewish person visits a synagogue, attends a Jewish religious ceremony (like a bar mitzvah or bat mitzvah — a coming-of-age celebration), or visits certain holy Jewish sites, they are often given a yarmulke to wear as a sign of respect for the space and the occasion. This is considered a polite, welcoming gesture, not a religious conversion of any kind. You simply put it on, participate respectfully, and return it when you leave.

A yarmulke is a small head cap worn by Jewish men (and sometimes women) as an expression of humility before God and as a marker of Jewish religious identity. It is one of the most recognizable symbols of Judaism, carrying both deep spiritual meaning and strong cultural significance.
17607: The word yarn has two separate meanings as a noun — one concrete and physical, the other informal and figurative. Both are important and widely used in English.
Meaning 1 — A Material: Twisted Strands of Fiber

Yarn is a long, continuous, thread-like strand made by twisting together many short, loose fibers. It is the fundamental raw material used to make fabric, clothing, blankets, scarves, and many other textiles.

Picture the soft, fluffy material wound into a ball that you would find in a craft store or in a grandmother's knitting basket. That is yarn.

What is yarn made from?

Yarn can come from natural sources or from synthetic (man-made) materials. Natural yarns include wool (from sheep), cotton (from the cotton plant), silk (from silkworms), cashmere (from goats), linen, and alpaca. Synthetic yarns include acrylic, polyester, nylon, and rayon. Different materials give different qualities — wool is warm and stretchy, cotton is cool and breathable, and acrylic is affordable and easy to wash.

How is yarn made?

Short, loose fibers are spun — that is, twisted — together to form a single continuous strand. Multiple strands can then be twisted together again to make the yarn thicker and more durable. This process of combining strands is called plying. When you see a yarn labeled "2-ply," it simply means two strands have been twisted together into one.

What is yarn used for?

Yarn is the starting material for knitting (using two long needles to loop yarn into fabric), crocheting (using a hook to form interlocked loops), weaving (threading yarn through a loom to create cloth), and various forms of needlework and embroidery.

How is yarn different from thread and string?

These three words confuse many learners, so here is a precise comparison:

Thread is much, much thinner than yarn. It is used in sewing machines or for hand-stitching to join pieces of fabric together. Think of the thin line you pass through a needle's eye to stitch a button back onto a shirt.

String is typically thicker and rougher than yarn, usually made from twisted plant fibers or synthetic material, and is used for tying or binding things — not for making cloth. Think of the string tied around a parcel.

Yarn is softer than string, thicker than thread, and its purpose is specifically for textile crafts such as knitting, weaving, and crocheting.

A useful way to picture the size order: thread → yarn → string → rope. Each one gets progressively thicker and rougher.

Thickness of yarn

Yarn comes in a range of thicknesses, which crafters refer to as "weight." The thinnest yarns (called lace or fingering weight) produce fine, delicate fabric. Medium yarns (called DK or worsted weight) are the most commonly used for everyday projects. The thickest yarns (called bulky or super bulky) create heavy, warm fabric very quickly. As a general rule: the thicker the yarn, the faster a project is completed, and the warmer the finished piece tends to be.
Meaning 2 — A Story: An Informal, Often Exaggerated Tale

In informal English, yarn also means a long, entertaining story — particularly one that is adventurous, colorful, or exciting in nature.

What makes a yarn different from just any story is its particular character. It is the kind of tale told in a relaxed, convivial setting — around a campfire, in a pub, on a ship's deck — where the storyteller brings it to life with great enthusiasm and dramatic flair. Crucially, a yarn is often exaggerated or embellished. The storyteller is likely stretching the truth somewhat to make the tale more gripping and entertaining. The listener usually knows this and enjoys it anyway.

Example: "The old sailor sat down and spun us a yarn about the enormous shark he once wrestled off the coast of Portugal."

The phrase spin a yarn is one of the most common idioms in English, and it means to tell one of these long, lively, embellished stories. If someone says, "He was spinning a yarn," they mean he was weaving an elaborate tale — and the implication is that the listener might be wise to take parts of it with a pinch of salt.

This second meaning of yarn is informal in register and is most commonly heard in British, Australian, and Irish English, though it is understood throughout the English-speaking world.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

Context makes this effortless:

If someone is talking about knitting, crocheting, a craft store, fabric, fibers, or textiles — they mean the physical material: long twisted strands of fiber.

If someone is talking about storytelling, a traveler's tale, an old sailor, a campfire, or something that might be exaggerated — they mean a long, entertaining, and possibly embellished story.

The two meanings never overlap in practice, so there is virtually no risk of confusion once you know both.
17608: A yashmak is a type of face veil traditionally worn by some Muslim women, most closely associated with Ottoman Turkey and certain parts of the broader Islamic world.

A yashmak is not a single piece of cloth. It is made up of two separate pieces of thin fabric — usually white or a light color — worn together on the face:

  • One piece covers the upper part of the face: from the forehead down to just above or at the bridge of the nose.
  • The other piece covers the lower part of the face: from just below the eyes, covering the nose, mouth, and chin.

When both pieces are in place, they overlap slightly in the middle, and the result is that only the eyes are left uncovered. Everything else — forehead, nose, cheeks, mouth, chin — is hidden behind the fabric.

The yashmak is rooted in the Islamic tradition of modesty (known more broadly as purdah or hijab — the general principle of modest covering for women in public). In cultures where this tradition was practiced strictly, women would cover not just their hair and body, but also their face when going out. The yashmak was the specific garment used to fulfill that face-covering requirement.

It was especially common during the Ottoman Empire era, where it was a standard part of a respectable woman's appearance in public.
How it differs from similar veils

This is important, because there are several kinds of face and head coverings in Islamic tradition, and they are not the same thing:

  • Hijab — covers the hair, ears, and neck, but leaves the face fully visible. Very widely worn today.
  • Niqab — a face veil that covers everything except the eyes, usually made of a single piece of fabric. Similar in effect to the yashmak, but typically one piece, not two.
  • Burqa — covers the entire body from head to toe, including the face, but with a mesh screen over the eye area so the woman can see out while remaining entirely hidden.
  • Yashmak — specifically a two-piece arrangement covering the face, leaving only the eyes exposed. Its defining feature is this double-cloth construction.

So the yashmak sits somewhere close to the niqab in terms of how much it covers, but it is a distinct garment with its own traditional form.
What it looks like in practice

Imagine a woman standing in a busy marketplace. She is wearing a long robe and a headscarf. But when you look at her face, you see only her eyes — the rest of her face is covered by two layers of thin, pale fabric that meet across the bridge of the nose. That is the yashmak. The fabric is usually fine and lightweight, not thick or heavy, so it is not suffocating to wear.

The yashmak, in its traditional Ottoman form, is largely historical today. It was most common in the 19th and early 20th centuries and declined as the Ottoman Empire gave way to modern Turkey, which moved toward more Westernized dress codes. However, the broader idea of face-covering veils continues in various forms (like the niqab) across different parts of the Muslim world.

You might encounter the word "yashmak" today primarily in:

  • Historical writing about the Ottoman period
  • Literature from the 19th or early 20th century
  • Dictionary or vocabulary contexts (as a relatively rare English word for a specific cultural garment)

A yashmak is a traditional veil made of two pieces of thin fabric, worn by some Muslim women to cover the face in public, leaving only the eyes visible — most historically associated with Ottoman Turkey.
17609:
Yaw is a specific type of rotational movement. It describes the side-to-side swinging of a moving object — its front (nose, bow, or tip) turning left or right around an imaginary vertical axis, like a spinning top rotating flat on a table.

The easiest way to picture it: stand still and shake your head "no." Your head rotates left, then right, around a vertical line running down your spine. That motion — horizontal rotation around a vertical axis — is exactly what yaw is.
The three rotations every vehicle can make

To understand yaw properly, you need to know that any vehicle in motion — an airplane, a ship, a rocket, a car — can rotate in three distinct ways. Each has its own name:

Pitch — the front tilts up or down. Think of nodding your head "yes," or a plane climbing or diving.

Roll — the vehicle tilts sideways along its length. Think of tilting your head toward your shoulder, or a plane banking to one side.

Yaw — the front swings left or right while the vehicle stays level. This is our word.

These three — pitch, roll, and yaw — are the complete vocabulary for describing how a vehicle is oriented in space. Yaw is always the horizontal, flat-spin rotation around the vertical axis.
What "yaw" refers to as a noun

As a noun, yaw can mean two related things:

  1. An instance of this side-to-side rotation — "The ship experienced a sudden yaw to port." This means the bow (front) of the ship swung to the left.
  2. The angle of that rotation — "A yaw of 15 degrees." This means the vehicle's nose has rotated 15 degrees away from the direction it was originally pointing.
Where you will meet this word

Aviation — In a plane, yaw is controlled by the rudder (the vertical fin at the tail). When the rudder deflects one way, the tail is pushed the opposite way, and the nose swings sideways. Pilots manage yaw carefully, especially during takeoff and landing. There is a well-known phenomenon called adverse yaw — when a pilot rolls the plane to one side, the nose involuntarily yaws in the opposite direction as a side effect. Correcting this is part of basic flying technique.

Ships and sailing — A ship yaws when waves, currents, or wind push its bow off the intended course. Holding a straight heading in rough seas requires constant correction against yaw. You might read: "Heavy swells caused the vessel to yaw unpredictably."

Spacecraft and missiles — Rockets and missiles must be carefully controlled in all three axes. A yaw during a rocket launch means the nose is pointing off the intended trajectory. Mission controllers track yaw in real time. A yaw maneuver is when a spacecraft intentionally rotates around its vertical axis — for example, to point an antenna toward Earth or align with a docking port.

Automotive engineering — Cars also yaw. When you turn a steering wheel, the car rotates around its vertical axis — that is yaw. Yaw rate is the technical term for how quickly this rotation is happening (measured in degrees per second). Too much yaw at high speed means the car is spinning out. Electronic stability control systems in modern cars work by measuring yaw rate and applying brakes to individual wheels to bring the car back under control.

Wind turbines — A wind turbine must always face directly into the wind to work efficiently. The mechanism that rotates the entire top of the turbine (the nacelle and blades) to track the wind is called the yaw system. When the turbine is not properly aligned with the wind, that misalignment is called yaw error.

Ballistics — A bullet is spin-stabilized (the rifling of a gun barrel makes it rotate rapidly along its flight axis, like a football spiral). A well-fired bullet has near-zero yaw — its nose points almost exactly in the direction of travel. But if the bullet is destabilized — by wind, imperfect firing, or impact with an object — its nose begins to swing off-axis. This is the bullet's yaw. Greater yaw means greater air resistance (drag) and less accuracy.
Key compound terms you will encounter

Yaw axis — the imaginary vertical line through the center of a vehicle, around which yaw rotation occurs.

Yaw rate — how fast the yaw rotation is happening, usually measured in degrees per second.

Yaw angle — the number of degrees a vehicle has rotated horizontally away from a reference direction (its original heading, or a target direction).

Yaw control — the systems responsible for managing and correcting yaw.

Yaw stability — a vehicle's natural tendency to resist unwanted yaw and return to its original heading. A vehicle with good yaw stability does not easily get pushed off course.

Adverse yaw — an unwanted yaw caused as a side effect of another maneuver (most commonly rolling an aircraft).
An important distinction: yaw is rotation, not travel

Yaw describes which way the vehicle is pointing, not necessarily which way it is moving. A ship can yaw 10 degrees to the right — meaning its bow rotates rightward — while still being carried forward (or even sideways) by momentum and currents. Similarly, a bullet can yaw (its nose tips sideways) while its overall path through the air barely changes. The rotation and the trajectory are separate things, even though uncontrolled yaw usually leads to a change in trajectory over time.

Yaw (noun) is the rotational movement of a vehicle or object around its vertical axis — the front (nose, bow, or tip) swings left or right while the vehicle remains otherwise level. It is one of the three fundamental axes of rotation (alongside pitch and roll) used in aviation, navigation, spacecraft engineering, automotive dynamics, and ballistics. As a noun, it names the specific type of motion itself, an instance of it occurring, or the angle by which the rotation has happened.
